newsitem.title: UK: EMU success hinges on labour market reform.
newsitem.headline: EMU success hinges on labour market reform.

text.p: The dream has always been compelling -- a unified Europe where money, goods and workers can move freely across borders.
The reality, economists say, is another matter -- differences in labour models and philosophies, only some of which will be bridged by 1999 when the euro single currency is due to start trading.
But Europe needs strict labour reforms to prevent a currency union from being strangled at birth by high unemployment.

"EMU is a good reason for countries to introduce flexible labour policies, which they will have to do anyway to reduce unemployment," said Jorgen Elmeskov, structural policy counsellor at the Paris-based OECD.
By 1999, euro "ins" should have armed themselves with more flexible labour policies and more moderate welfare systems if they are to survive in an environment where competition will run wild.

But progress in this vote-sensitive territory will be slow, and generous wages and social benefits threaten to undermine European economic and monetary union (EMU) even if political will may push it through, economists say.
Many EMU candidate governments have committed themselves to tightening the fiscal screws at a time when unemployment is running in double-digits, public debt is spiralling and populations are ageing.
BITTER PILLS

Economists say that set against such a gloomy background, EMU is certain to backfire unless structural unemployment is cured and even then, unemployment is likely to stay high in the first years of the euro.

"EMU will go ahead no matter how rigid or flexible labour markets are, but whether it will become a success or not will depend largely on whether these structural issues are tackled," said Joachim Fels, senior economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
Governments have little room for manoeuvre.

Stripped of control over such a key economic lever as interest rates when monetary reins are surrendered to the European Central Bank, they may have little choice but to free labour markets from state control.
In any case, rock-bottom interest rates have also failed to jolt the European economy.

Few governments have seemed ready to take the plunge, analysts say. While the Dutch have reformed their labour markets, Germany and France are treading carefully for fear of causing social unrest, and hampering EMU.

Germany's fragile centre-right coalition lacks the power to push through major reform measures, and the new French socialist government, grappling with 12.5 percent unemployment, is wary of the whole idea.
"The trouble is that France in particular, and Germany to a lesser extent, don't accept the labour flexibility model," said Adrian Schmidt, senior international economist at Chase here.
The German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said euro hopefuls should focus on reducing structural unemployment without committing new funds.
But French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin is boxed in by election promises to create jobs and has already agreed to raise France's minimum wage -- a move economists scorn.
At a summit in Amsterdam in June France secured a European resolution emphasising the importance of jobs, but the details have not been worked out.
Although French wages are not as high as those in Germany, the labour market is more rigid and the public sector, shielded from competition, weighs more heavily on the budget, analysts said.
Germany has made some strides. Companies are already undercutting high wages that thrive on state-backed contracts, and working hours are expected to be reduced.
"The wage cartel that we had in Germany for a long time is breaking down," said Fels.

But a stumbling block is the welfare sector where the government will struggle to overhaul high social benefits and pension payments, economists say. One bright spot is Italy, where Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government, desperate to join the euro in the first wave, has embarked on plans to reform the state pension scheme. With a rapidly ageing population, pension expenditure in Italy -- the biggest in Europe at some 62 percent of the total welfare bill -- is forecast to rise to unsustainable levels unless significant reforms are implemented.

Overall continental European labour has lagged behind the United States, whose flexible job markets set a model for the rest of the world, and Britain, where nearly two decades of right-wing rule emasculated labour unions and encouraged mobility.
Both the U.S. and British economies are growing at a healthy speed while the rest of Europe is crawling.
THE WRONG DIAGNOSIS?

Not all economists subscribe to the view that Europe's unemployment is structural. Some argue that the double blow of debt and unemployment is symptomatic of recession, and labour flexibility cannot cure it alone.
"The idea in Europe that unemployment is structural is very weak and I don't believe it," said Chris Allsopp, lecturer in economics at New College, Oxford.
"If you're going to get rid of the twin crises you need really to raise the European growth rate by 0.5 to 1.0 percent a year over the next decade," he said.
That in itself is a formidable task, but Allsopp said the solution was a careful blend of fiscal consolidation, monetary softening, and a weak exchange rate.
Others say that while growth can help stem further job losses, it will be insufficient to take those who are already unemployed off the dole.
